description: We are a team of creative, curious, and passionate individuals interested in technology, science, and innovation. We are motivated by learning, sharing knowledge, and working together to develop ideas that can become solutions to real-world problems. We are looking for committed people with initiative, critical thinking, creativity, and skills in programming, design, research, or data analysis who are excited to take on new challenges and be part of this experience.
summary:
SPACE LEGACY is an interactive digital museum about the machines humanity has left on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. It was created in response to the NASA Space Apps Challenge "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," built on a simple idea: "abandoned" does not mean "forgotten."

The site brings together a 3D rover viewer, a multimedia center connected to NASA's official library, and the educational game "Rastro de Exploradores" (Trail of Explorers). The game has four missions based on real equipment: driving the Lunar Rover, flying the Ingenuity helicopter, locating a marsquake like InSight, and pointing Voyager 1's antenna toward Earth. Each completed mission earns a stamp in an exploration passport, and completing all four earns a diploma.

Our goal is to bring space exploration closer to students and the general public, especially Spanish speakers, by turning hard-to-read data into an experience that teaches real science. It works in Spanish and English, on computers, tablets, and phones, with nothing to install and no account needed.

It was developed by the Tripulación 404 team using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and it relies on official NASA resources and data, with visible credits.
details:
SPACE LEGACY is an interactive digital museum about the machines humanity has left on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space. It includes a 3D rover viewer, a multimedia center connected to NASA’s library, and the game “Explorers’ Trail,” featuring four missions based on real spacecraft: driving the Lunar Rover, piloting the Ingenuity helicopter, detecting a seismic event like InSight, and pointing Voyager 1’s antenna toward Earth. Each mission earns a stamp in an exploration passport, and upon completing all four, a diploma.

It transforms data that is usually presented in a table into a playful experience: each mission teaches a real scientific concept, such as signal delay in deep space. It works in Spanish and English, on any device, without requiring any installation or account creation. It aims to bring space exploration closer to students and the general public: “abandoned” does not mean “forgotten.”

It’s built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript without frameworks, using Canvas for missions, Google’s Model Viewer for 3D models, and the NASA Image and Video Library API. It saves language settings and progress in the browser without collecting personal data. We tested it with Playwright and used Claude to assist with programming, testing, and writing.

It’s creative because it shifts the focus from “what NASA did” to “what it left behind and why it matters,” and each mini-game replicates real science. We prioritize accessibility, scientific rigor, and fallback options in case an external resource fails.
dataRefs: The descent stages of the Lunar Modules (such as the Apollo 11 *Eagle*) were left behind to serve as launch platforms.
The first rover on Mars (1997), delivered by the Pathfinder lander. It is currently permanently stationed there.
Two twin exploratory vehicles that remained in operation for years. Both are now inactive monuments to the exploration of Mars.
Three electric "lunar vehicle"-type craft, driven by astronauts. Permanently parked on the Moon.
Lunar surface experiment packages from the Apollo program (seismometers, retroreflectors, etc.) that were left behind to conduct scientific research after the astronauts' departure.
The first aircraft on another planet. It sustained damage to its rotor and became a stationary object.
